SNAP's improper payment rate hit 10.62% last year, more than three times its 2013 low. The reason is structural: states run the program but federal taxpayers cover 90% of costs, giving states little incentive to crack down on errors, notes Cato's @RominaBoccia and Tyler Turman.

Learn more: ow.ly/auag50ZlGu2

Juries aren't rubber stamps—they're a constitutional check on government power. Georgia's Supreme Court just said so plainly in Clark v. Leigh: jury verdicts must carry real legal force, or the right to a jury trial is "hollow and illusory," explains Cato's Matthew Cavedon.
ow.ly/Tnxy50ZlCTo

Recovering the Historical Jury: The Georgia Supreme Court Points the Way

The Clark case arose after a Georgia woman died from surgery complications.

By most any measure, the United States has the most expensive health sector in the world. 

Removing government barriers to new providers would expand patient access, increase choice, and help make health care more affordable. 

Cato scholars propose immediate, supply-side policy changes that would broaden choice and improve affordability. Check out the Cato Institute Handbook on Affordability: ow.ly/kIww50Z5BV5

The Supreme Court left election rules where the Constitution puts them: with the states. In upholding mail ballot grace periods, the Court didn't expand federal power or ballot counting timelines. Most of the loudest online reactions got the ruling wrong, notes Cato’s @stephen_richer.

ow.ly/KJ2p50ZlhBI

Link



What the Supreme Court's Mail Ballot Decision Doesn't Mean

The court neither asserted states’ control over elections nor blessed the slow counting of ballots.
